idiom_name: Vapor AsyncMiddleware authorization guard over the authenticated User, with a Fluent Role model and UserRole pivot for the assignment matrix
implementation_notes: Vapor ships authentication (the Authenticator chain, GuardMiddleware, req.auth.get(User.self)) but no role model, so RBAC is written by hand on top of it. Model roles as data - a Fluent Role (name) with a UserRole sibling/pivot carrying the assignment and a User -> roles relation - and enforce with a middleware (or a route group) that resolves the authenticated user's roles and compares them against the roles the route requires, throwing Abort(.forbidden) on denial. GuardMiddleware only proves the user is authenticated, never that it holds a role, so the role check is a second middleware placed after it. Grouping protected routes under app.grouped(User.guardMiddleware(), RequireRole(required: ["pauser"])) is the deny-by-default seam: an endpoint inside the group is protected, and the discipline is to keep the tree rather than sprinkle checks. Grant/revoke is a Fluent write to the pivot inside a governed admin route, and the middleware reads roles from the database per request (cached) rather than from anything the client sends.
pitfalls: GuardMiddleware proves authentication only; a route group with just User.guardMiddleware() is open to every authenticated user, so the role check needs its own middleware.
Resolving the user's roles from the database on every request is the usual cost; cache the resolution per request (or session) and invalidate on assignment change.
Reading roles from the request body or a custom header lets the caller escalate; only req.auth (populated by an Authenticator) counts as the subject.
Middleware ordering matters: a role guard placed before the authenticator sees no user and denies everything, and one placed after an error/redirect middleware may never run.
A Fluent pivot without a unique constraint on (user_id, role_id) allows duplicate assignments that skew counts and complicate revocation.
